title: integration testing databases webapplicationfactory and contracts
concepts: Integration tests exercise the behavior of two or more components together, including infrastructure boundaries that isolated unit tests intentionally replace.

An in-memory TestServer and a real Kestrel process exercise different boundaries. TestServer is fast and deterministic for application-pipeline behavior; real sockets, TLS, reverse proxies, containers, or deployment settings require an appropriate end-to-end environment.

WebApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint> bootstraps an ASP.NET Core application for tests. A custom factory can override configuration and services, but replacing too much production wiring weakens the test.

Each test run needs deliberate database isolation. Unique databases, schemas, transactions, disposable containers, or reset scripts have distinct limits when tests execute concurrently or use multiple connections.

Contract tests verify an agreed interface between a provider and consumer. They complement integration tests and should be used where independently deployed services need compatible request, response, and failure semantics.

Integration tests are slower and more environment-sensitive than unit tests; keep assertions focused on observable cross-component behavior, make dependencies explicit, and collect diagnostics on failure.

accuracyFacts: WebApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint> typically creates an in-process TestServer. This exercises application hosting and middleware behavior without proving real socket, TLS, reverse-proxy, DNS, or deployment behavior; use an appropriate real-process environment for those boundaries.

The ASP.NET Core integration-testing guidance commonly uses Development as the test host environment when no environment is set. Tests should set the intended environment explicitly when environment-specific configuration matters.

EF Core InMemory is non-relational: it does not support transactions or raw SQL and can differ from production query behavior. Microsoft discourages it as a general database fake. SQLite in-memory is relational but still differs from the production provider; provider-specific queries and semantics require tests against the production database engine.

EF Core recommends testing against the production database system for database behavior where practical. Test doubles remain useful for narrowly controlled scenarios, but passing against a double does not prove production-provider behavior.

An in-memory SQLite database is tied to an open connection; closing the connection deletes the database. Tests that need multiple contexts to share it must keep the connection open for the test lifetime.
Testcontainers wait strategies establish a readiness condition; a running container or open mapped port alone does not prove that the application inside is ready to serve the tested behavior.

Pact-style consumer/provider contract tests use a simulated provider during consumer verification and provider verification against the provider implementation. They test interactions captured in contracts, not every behavior of the whole distributed system.

A loopback HTTP server such as WireMock.Net exercises real HTTP serialization and request handling from the client perspective; an HttpMessageHandler stub is narrower and does not exercise sockets, HTTP framing, or server behavior.

Database isolation strategy must account for all connections, background work, transactions, parallel tests, and cleanup. A transaction around the test is insufficient when application code uses an independent connection or commits outside that transaction.

Logs, dumps, request bodies, database snapshots, and container output can contain secrets or personal data. Capture only what is needed and apply the repository's artifact-access and retention policy.

PactNet provider verification requires the provider to be reachable over a real TCP socket; the PactNet project warns that ASP.NET Core TestServer/WebApplicationFactory in-process hosting cannot be used for provider verification.
